sword_marker_records.content_osis: <div sID="gen15849" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="17" osisID="Isa.17" sID="Isa.17"/> <div eID="gen15849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15850" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15851" type="x-p"/> Syria and Ephraim were confederate against Judah (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.1-Isa.7.2">ch. vii. 1, 2</reference>), and, they being so closely linked together in their counsels, this chapter, though it be entitled "the burden of Damascus" (which was the head city of Syria), reads the doom of Israel too. I. The destruction of the strong cities both of Syria and Israel is here foretold, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1-Isa.17.5">ver. 1-5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.17.9-Isa.17.11">ver. 9-11</reference>. II. In the midst of judgment mercy is remembered to Israel, and a gracious promise made that a remnant should be preserved from the calamities and should get good by them, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.6-Isa.17.8">ver. 6-8</reference>. III. The overthrow of the Assyrian army before Jerusalem is pointed at, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.12-Isa.17.14">ver. 12-14</reference>. In order of time this chapter should be placed next after <reference osisRef="Isa.19.1-Isa.19.25">ch. ix.</reference>, for the destruction of Damascus, here foretold, happened in the reign of Ahaz, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2 Kings xvi. 9</reference>.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen15853" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of Syria and Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 712.)</title> <div sID="gen15854" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Yet gleaning grapes shall be left in it, as the shaking of an olive tree, two <hi type="italic">or</hi> three berries in the top of the uppermost bough, four <hi type="italic">or</hi> five in the outmost fruitful branches thereof, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel. <hi type="super">7</hi> At that day shall a man look to his Maker, and his eyes shall have respect to the Holy One of Israel. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he shall not look to the altars, the work of his hands, neither shall respect <hi type="italic">that</hi> which his fingers have made, either the groves, or the images. <div eID="gen15854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15855" type="x-p"/> Mercy is here reserved, in a parenthesis, in the midst of judgment, for a remnant that should escape the common ruin of the kingdom of the ten tribes. Though the Assyrians took all the care they could that none should slip out of their net, yet the meek of the earth were hidden in the day of the Lord's anger, and had their lives given them for a prey and made comfortable to them by their retirement to the land of Judah, where they had the liberty of God's courts. 1. They shall be but a small remnant, a very few, who shall be marked for preservation (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Gleaning grapes shall be left in it.</hi> The body of the people were carried into captivity, but here and there one was left behind, perhaps one of two in a bed when the other was taken, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.34">Luke xvii. 34</reference>. The most desolating judgments in this world are short of the last judgment, which shall be universal and which none shall escape. In times of the greatest calamity some are kept safe, as in times of the greatest degeneracy some are kept pure. But the fewness of those that escape supposes the captivity of the far greatest part; those that are left are but like the poor remains of an olive tree when it has been carefully shaken by the owner; if there be <hi type="italic">two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough</hi> (out of the reach of those that shook it), that is all. Such is the <hi type="italic">remnant according to the election of grace,</hi> very few in comparison with the multitudes that walk on in the broad way. 2. They shall be a sanctified remnant, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.7-Isa.17.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. These few that are preserved are such as, in the prospect of the judgment approaching, had repented of their sins and reformed their lives, and therefore were snatched thus as brands out of the burning, or such as having escaped, and becoming refugees in strange countries, were awakened, partly by a sense of the distinguishing mercy of their deliverance, and partly by the distresses they were still in, to return to God. (1.) They shall look up to their Creator, shall enquire, <hi type="italic">Where is God my Maker, who giveth songs in the night,</hi> in such a night of affliction as this? <reference osisRef="Job.35.10-Job.35.11">Job xxxv. 10, 11</reference>. They shall acknowledge his hand in all the events concerning them, merciful and afflictive, and shall submit to his hand. They shall give him the glory due to his name, and be suitably affected with his providences. They shall expect relief and succour from him and depend upon him to help them. Their <hi type="italic">eyes shall have respect</hi> to him, <hi type="italic">as the eyes of a servant to the hand of his master,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.132.2">Ps. cxxiii. 2</reference>. Observe, It is our duty at all times to have respect to God, to have our eyes ever towards him, both as our Maker (the author of our being and the God of nature) and as the Holy One of Israel, a God in covenant with us and the God of grace; particularly, when we are in affliction, our eyes must be towards the Lord, to <hi type="italic">pluck our feet out of the net</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.15">Ps. xxv. 15</reference>); to bring us to this is the design of his providence as he is our Maker and the work of his grace as he is the Holy One of Israel. (2.) They shall look off from their idols, the creatures of their own fancy, shall no longer worship them, and seek to them, and expect relief from them. For God will be alone regarded, or he does not look upon himself as at all regarded. He that looks to his Maker must not <hi type="italic">look to the altars, the work of his hands,</hi> but disown them and cast them off, must not retain the least respect for <hi type="italic">that which his fingers have made,</hi> but break it to pieces, though it be his own workmanship—<hi type="italic">the groves and the images;</hi> the word signifies images made in honour of the sun and by which he was worshipped, the most ancient and most plausible idolatry, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.19">Deut. iv. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job xxxi. 26</reference>. We have reason to account those happy afflictions which part between us and our sins, and by sensible convictions of the vanity of the world, that great idol, cool our affections to it and lower our expectations from it.

But the fewness of those that escape supposes the captivity of the far greatest part; those that are left are but like the poor remains of an olive tree when it has been carefully shaken by the owner; if there be two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough (out of the reach of those that shook it), that is all. Such is the remnant according to the election of grace, very few in comparison with the multitudes that walk on in the broad way. 2. They shall be a sanctified remnant, v. 7, 8 . These few that are preserved are such as, in the prospect of the judgment approaching, had repented of their sins and reformed their lives, and therefore were snatched thus as brands out of the burning, or such as having escaped, and becoming refugees in strange countries, were awakened, partly by a sense of the distinguishing mercy of their deliverance, and partly by the distresses they were still in, to return to God. (1.) They shall look up to their Creator, shall enquire, Where is God my Maker, who giveth songs in the night, in such a night of affliction as this? Job xxxv. 10, 11 . They shall acknowledge his hand in all the events concerning them, merciful and afflictive, and shall submit to his hand. They shall give him the glory due to his name, and be suitably affected with his providences. They shall expect relief and succour from him and depend upon him to help them. Their eyes shall have respect to him, as the eyes of a servant to the hand of his master, Ps. cxxiii. 2 . Observe, It is our duty at all times to have respect to God, to have our eyes ever towards him, both as our Maker (the author of our being and the God of nature) and as the Holy One of Israel, a God in covenant with us and the God of grace; particularly, when we are in affliction, our eyes must be towards the Lord, to pluck our feet out of the net ( Ps. xxv. 15 ); to bring us to this is the design of his providence as he is our Maker and the work of his grace as he is the Holy One of Israel. (2.) They shall look off from their idols, the creatures of their own fancy, shall no longer worship them, and seek to them, and expect relief from them. For God will be alone regarded, or he does not look upon himself as at all regarded. He that looks to his Maker must not look to the altars, the work of his hands, but disown them and cast them off, must not retain the least respect for that which his fingers have made, but break it to pieces, though it be his own workmanship— the groves and the images; the word signifies images made in honour of the sun and by which he was worshipped, the most ancient and most plausible idolatry, Deut. iv. 19 ; Job xxxi. 26 . That the cities should be deserted. Even the strong cities, which should have protected the country, shall not be able to protect themselves: They <hi type="italic">shall be as a forsaken bough and an uppermost branch</hi> of an old tree, which has gone to decay, is forsaken of its leaves, and appears on the top of the tree, bare, and dry, and dead; so shall their strong cities look when the inhabitants have deserted them and the victorious army of the enemy pillaged and defaced them, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.9">v. 9</reference>. They shall be as the cities (so it may be supplied) which the Canaanites left, the old inhabitants of the land, because of the children of Israel, when God brought them in with a high hand, to take possession of that good land, cities which they built not. As the Canaanites then fled before Israel, so Israel should now flee before the Assyrians. That the country should be laid waste, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.10-Isa.17.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. Observe here, (1.) The sin that had provoked God to bring so great a destruction upon that pleasant land. It was <hi type="italic">for the iniquity of those that dwelt therein.</hi> "It is <hi type="italic">because thou hast forgotten the God of thy salvation</hi> and all the great salvations he has wrought for thee, hast forgotten thy dependence upon him and obligations to him, and <hi type="italic">hast not been mindful of the rock of thy strength,</hi> not only who is himself a strong rock, but who has been thy strength many a time, or thou wouldst have been sunk and broken long since." (2.) The destruction itself, aggravated by the great care they took to improve their land and to make it yet more pleasant. [1.] Look upon it at the time of the seedness, and it was all like a garden and a vineyard; that pleasant land was replenished with pleasant plants, the choicest of its own growth; nay, so nice and curious were the inhabitants that, not content with them, they sent to all the neighbouring countries for strange slips, the more valuable for being strange, uncommon, far-fetched, and dear-bought, though perhaps they had of their own not inferior to them. This was an instance of their pride and vanity, and (that ruining error) their affection to be <hi type="italic">like the nations. Wheat, and honey, and oil</hi> were their staple commodities (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.17">Ezek. xxvii. 17</reference>); but, not content with these, they must have flowers and greens with strange names imported from other nations, and a great deal of care and pains must be taken by hot-beds to make these plants to grow; the soil must be forced, and they must be covered with glasses to shelter them, and early in the morning the gardeners must be up to make the seed to flourish, that it may excel those of their neighbours. entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen15857" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of Syria and Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 712.)</title> <div sID="gen15858" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Woe to the multitude of many people, <hi type="italic">which</hi> make a noise like the noise of the seas; and to the rushing of nations, <hi type="italic">that</hi> make a rushing like the rushing of mighty waters! <hi type="super">13</hi> The nations shall rush like the rushing of many waters: but <hi type="italic">God</hi> shall rebuke them, and they shall flee far off, and shall be chased as the chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind. <hi type="super">14</hi> And behold at evening tide trouble; <hi type="italic">and</hi> before the morning he <hi type="italic">is</hi> not. This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the portion of them that spoil us, and the lot of them that rob us. <div eID="gen15858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15859" type="x-p"/> These verses read the doom of those that spoil and rob the people of God. If the Assyrians and Israelites invade and plunder Judah, if the Assyrian army take God's people captive and lay their country waste, let them know that ruin will be their lot and portion. They are here brought in, 1. Triumphing over the people of God. They relied upon their numbers. The Assyrian army was made up out of divers nations: it was <hi type="italic">the multitude of many people</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.12">v. 12</reference>), by which weight they hoped to carry the cause. They were very noisy, like the roaring of the seas; they talked big, hectored, and threatened, to frighten God's people from resisting them, and all their allies from sending in to their aid. Sennacherib and Rabshakeh, in their speeches and letters, made a mighty noise to strike a terror upon Hezekiah and his people; the nations that followed them <hi type="italic">made a rushing like the rushing of many waters,</hi> and those mighty ones, that threaten to bear down all before them and carry away every thing that stands in their way. <hi type="italic">The floods have lifted up their voice, have lifted up their waves;</hi> such is the tumult of the people, and the heathen, when they rage, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.1">Ps. ii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.93.3">xciii. 3</reference>. 2. Triumphed over by the judgments of God. They thought to carry their point by dint of noise; but woe to them (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.12">v. 12</reference>), for he <hi type="italic">shall rebuke them,</hi> that is, God shall, one whom they little think of, have no regard to, stand in no awe of; he shall give them a check with an invisible hand, <hi type="italic">and</hi> then <hi type="italic">they shall flee afar off.</hi> Sennacherib, and Rabshakeh, and the remains of their forces, shall run away in a fright, and shall be chased by their own terrors, <hi type="italic">as the chaff of the mountains</hi> which stand bleak <hi type="italic">before the wind, and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind,</hi> like thistle-down (so the margin); they make themselves <hi type="italic">as chaff before the wind</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.5">Ps. xxxv. 5</reference>) and then <hi type="italic">the angel of the Lord</hi> (as it follows there), the same angel that slew many of them, shall chase the rest. God will make <hi type="italic">them like a wheel,</hi> or rolling thing, and then <hi type="italic">persecute them with his tempest</hi> and <hi type="italic">make them afraid with his storm,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.83.13">Ps. lxxxiii. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.83.15">15</reference>. Note, God can dispirit the enemies of his church when they are most courageous and confident, and dissipate them when they seem most closely consolidated. This shall be done suddenly (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">At evening-tide</hi> they are very troublesome, and threaten trouble to the people of God; but <hi type="italic">before the morning they are not.</hi> At sleeping time they are cast into a deep sleep, <reference osisRef="Ps.26.5-Ps.26.6">Ps. xxvi. 5, 6</reference>. It was in the night that the angel routed the Assyrian army. God can in a moment break the power of his church's enemies, even when it appears most formidable; and this is written for the encouragement of the people of God in all ages, when they find themselves an unequal match for their enemies; for <hi type="italic">this is the portion of those that spoil us,</hi> they shall themselves be spoiled. God will plead his church's cause, and those that meddle do it to their own hurt.  <chapter eID="Isa.17"/> <div eID="gen15859" type="x-p"/>

They thought to carry their point by dint of noise; but woe to them ( v. 12 ), for he shall rebuke them, that is, God shall, one whom they little think of, have no regard to, stand in no awe of; he shall give them a check with an invisible hand, and then they shall flee afar off. Sennacherib, and Rabshakeh, and the remains of their forces, shall run away in a fright, and shall be chased by their own terrors, as the chaff of the mountains which stand bleak before the wind, and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind, like thistle-down (so the margin); they make themselves as chaff before the wind ( Ps. xxxv. 5 ) and then the angel of the Lord (as it follows there), the same angel that slew many of them, shall chase the rest. God will make them like a wheel, or rolling thing, and then persecute them with his tempest and make them afraid with his storm, Ps. lxxxiii. 13 , 15 . Note, God can dispirit the enemies of his church when they are most courageous and confident, and dissipate them when they seem most closely consolidated. This shall be done suddenly ( v. 14 ): At evening-tide they are very troublesome, and threaten trouble to the people of God; but before the morning they are not. At sleeping time they are cast into a deep sleep, Ps. xxvi. 5, 6 . It was in the night that the angel routed the Assyrian army. God can in a moment break the power of his church's enemies, even when it appears most formidable; and this is written for the encouragement of the people of God in all ages, when they find themselves an unequal match for their enemies; for this is the portion of those that spoil us, they shall themselves be spoiled. God will plead his church's cause, and those that meddle do it to their own hurt.

( b. c. 712.) 12 Woe to the multitude of many people, which make a noise like the noise of the seas; and to the rushing of nations, that make a rushing like the rushing of mighty waters! 13 The nations shall rush like the rushing of many waters: but God shall rebuke them, and they shall flee far off, and shall be chased as the chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind. 14 And behold at evening tide trouble; and before the morning he is not. This is the portion of them that spoil us, and the lot of them that rob us. These verses read the doom of those that spoil and rob the people of God. If the Assyrians and Israelites invade and plunder Judah, if the Assyrian army take God's people captive and lay their country waste, let them know that ruin will be their lot and portion. They are here brought in, 1. Triumphing over the people of God. They relied upon their numbers. navigation_sections.title: Isaiah 17 · Original chapter introduction
navigation_sections.content_plain: Syria and Ephraim were confederate against Judah ( ch. vii. 1, 2 ), and, they being so closely linked together in their counsels, this chapter, though it be entitled "the burden of Damascus" (which was the head city of Syria), reads the doom of Israel too. I. The destruction of the strong cities both of Syria and Israel is here foretold, ver. 1-5 and ver. 9-11 . II. In the midst of judgment mercy is remembered to Israel, and a gracious promise made that a remnant should be preserved from the calamities and should get good by them, ver. 6-8 . III. The overthrow of the Assyrian army before Jerusalem is pointed at, ver. 12-14 . In order of time this chapter should be placed next after ch. ix. , for the destruction of Damascus, here foretold, happened in the reign of Ahaz, 2 Kings xvi. 9 .
